claim: None of the three locative púr- passages places a human population inside a fort as a statement of fact: RV 2.35.6 has a deity dwelling far off in 'raw' or 'unbaked' purs, and RV 6.2.7 and 9.107.10 are both explicit similes - 'like an old man in a fort', 'as a man enters the fort'.

notes: Read as evidence that a púr was uninhabited this row would be misused, and DJ-I-02 says why: a simile draws on the ordinary, so 'like an old man in a fort' presupposes for its audience exactly the inhabited fort the corpus never asserts. The two similes are evidence FOR habitability. Recorded here as a measurement of what the passages are, with the inference left to the interpretation register.

claim: No lemma in the Rigveda is glossed 'brick' (Ziegel) and none is glossed 'city' (Stadt), against a denominator of 9,196 of the corpus's 10,031 lemmas carrying a Grassmann gloss - 91.7% of lemmas and 78.98% of tokens.
locator: 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-nandi-gate.py, section 'ARCHITECTURE VOCABULARY'; probes ziegel / stadt, städt over info/matched_lemmata.json
notes: Typed under the negative-evidence standard in DJ-009; NOT a finding about Rigvedic society on its own. Three limits travel with it and are not optional. (1) The 835 unglossed lemmas are overwhelmingly verbal roots and particles - √as- 1, √kr̥-, √dhā- 1, √bhū-, íd - so the gap is unlikely to hide a noun for brick, but it is not empty. (2) The probes are German because Grassmann wrote German; a handful of his glosses are Latin and are not reached. (3) Per DEP-005 the lemma and the gloss are ONE source, so this is Grassmann's lexicon reporting an absence, not the corpus doing so unmediated.

claim: The absence of a brick word from the Rigveda is typed ABSENT DESPITE ADEQUATE SEARCH for the lexicon as glossed, and NOT PRODUCED for the historical question: the corpus is liturgical praise poetry that nowhere describes construction technique for any structure, so a term for a building material had low probability of being produced in it whatever the material was.
locator: Negative-evidence standard, CLAUDE.md; evidence base DJ-008; the coverage figure is the search adequacy and the genre is the production probability
notes: The distinction is load-bearing and cuts against the use this measurement would most readily be put to. ABSENT DESPITE ADEQUATE SEARCH is a statement about this lexicon; NOT PRODUCED is a statement about what a hymn corpus was ever going to contain. An argument that the Rigvedic people did not know brick CANNOT be built on this row. What the row does support is narrower and is in DJ-I-01: the corpus supplies no positive lexical evidence of brick architecture, so an argument that supplies it must come from somewhere else.

claim: All 21 durgá- tokens in the Rigveda are neuter, and none denotes a fortification. Every one means difficult ground, a rough place or a peril, and the recurrent construction is a prayer to be carried across or out of one - six of the 21 are the same refrain at RV 1.106.1-6, 'as a chariot from a difficult ravine'.
locator: 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-nandi-gate.py, section 'EVERY durgá- TOKEN'; the 21 stanzas listed there; Griffith at each; gender=N on all 21 in the SRC-022 morphology
notes: The Classical Sanskrit sense 'fortress' for durga- is not in evidence in this corpus on this lexicon, and no token is broken, besieged, entered or held. This is the §7 audit doing its work on an inherited English category: 'fort' imported into durgá- from a later stratum of the language is exactly what the translation standard exists to catch. It remains Grassmann's lexicon plus Griffith's renderings - two nineteenth-century European sources, DEP-021 - and a reading of these 21 passages from an edition with a commentary could move it.

claim: The corpus does carry settlement and dwelling vocabulary, and it is not the fort word: víś- 'Niederlassung, Ansiedlung einer Familie, Clansdorf' at 200 tokens, kṣáya- 'Wohnung' 70, gr̥há- 'Haus' 69, vr̥jána- 'Gemeinschaft, Territorium' 61, grā́ma- 'Treck, Heerhaufen, Kriegerschar, wehrhafte Mannschaft einer Siedlung' 9.
locator: 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-nandi-gate.py, sections 'ARCHITECTURE VOCABULARY' rows house/dwelling and village/settlement
notes: Recorded so that DJ-008's two absences are not read as an absence of settlement vocabulary in general. The corpus has plenty; what it lacks is a word its own nineteenth-century lexicographer rendered 'city' or 'brick'. grā́ma- is worth its own note: Grassmann's Rigvedic gloss makes it a moving war-band, not a village, which is a second inherited English category failing the same way durgá- does in DJ-011.
